Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Ukraine’s Zelensky says U.S. envoys floated Kyiv ceding Donbas to Russia in exchange for NATO membership, a proposal he says would be put to the Ukrainian people if formally offered.
• The White House says Trump, Putin and Xi plan a historic joint meeting in China next week, with nuclear arms reduction on the agenda.
• Hungary’s new government uncovered $20m during a probe of an Orbán-era minister amid a promised anti-corruption drive.
• South Sudan postponed its first national elections to February 11.
• Zelensky accused SpaceX of “political” throttling of Starshield services affecting Ukrainian drones along the frontline.
Why it matters: Diplomacy around Ukraine, a rare Trump–Xi–Putin summit, and governance shifts in Hungary and South Sudan signal potential inflection points for European security and democratic transitions.

Science & Technology
• Microsoft said Outlook, Teams, and Copilot services were fully restored after a day-long global outage, attributing the disruption to a bad update.

• The FAA lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop, citing obsolete equipment; officials plan broader upgrades.
• Scientists built the first quantum clock powered by sunlight, hinting at field-ready precision timekeeping.
Why it matters: Resilience of critical IT and aviation infrastructure and advances in spaceflight and metrology will shape reliability and innovation across industries.

Entertainment.title: Jamie Pearl on the Art of Photographing Fame
Entertainment.text: SummaryJamie Pearl reflects on capturing candid moments with Doechii, Dennis Rodman, Nina Dobrev and other cultural figures.From spontaneous celebrity portraits to experimental editorial work, the photographer shares a creative approach shaped by energy, instinct and authenticity.Some of the most memorable celebrity photographs happen when no one's quite ready for the camera. A cigarette break outside a Fashion Week dinner, a fleeting moment in the backseat of a car, or the final touches before a red carpet appearance can reveal more personality than a carefully staged portrait. For New York-based photographer Jamie Pearl, those in-between moments have become the foundation of a practice rooted in spontaneity and human connection.After discovering black-and-white film photography in high school, Jamie eventually found a footing in New York's fashion and entertainment circles, capturing everyone from Dennis Rodman and Doechii to Keke Palmer and Nina Dobrev. While the fast-paced world of celebrity events has sharpened an instinct for the unexpected, a growing interest in editorial photography has opened up new possibilities for creative experimentation. We caught up with Jamie to discuss memorable encounters, the art of thinking on your feet, and why the best images often happen when you least expect them."In the words of one of my favorite photographers, Tyrell Hampton, it’s all about energy."How did you first get into photography, and when did you start shooting celebrities?I first got into photography about 13 years ago, when I was a 15-year-old high school student. I attended an arts-focused high school, which I credit with so much of my creative development. I always knew I was an artist, but when my drawings weren’t turning out quite how I envisioned them in my head, and I realized I didn’t exactly have a knack for playing the piano, I knew I needed to do some exploring to find my medium. Luckily, going to a high school that offered such a wide range of art classes made that pretty easy. I discovered black-and-white film photography during my sophomore year and quickly realized that lens-based mediums were what I wanted to pursue.I started photographing celebrities about a year after moving to New York in 2022. One of my earliest experiences was documenting Nelly Furtado and Justin Timberlake’s looks ahead of the VMAs, which sparked my love for what has since become some of my favorite work: intimate, pre-event, “get ready with me”-style photography.What usually catches your eye when you're photographing someone?In the words of one of my favorite photographers, Tyrell Hampton, it’s all about energy. Tyrell spoke about this so eloquently in an interview a while back, and I remember thinking how perfectly he had put into words something I’d always felt but never quite knew how to articulate. It’s so true. I’m constantly drawn to the energy people bring into a room, whether it’s the excitement of greeting their friends, going crazy on the dance floor, or feeling themselves in the bathroom mirror while touching up their lip liner."I’ve found myself craving more space to be deliberate with my images."Do you usually have a shot in mind, or do you prefer to let things happen naturally? The biggest thing I’ve learned from my years of event and spontaneous photography is that you can plan a shot all you want, but in those settings, you often have to adapt to whatever the talent has the time and bandwidth for. Sure, I’d love to have 10 minutes to pull someone aside to a cool corner of a bar and take their portrait, but realistically, there are plenty of times when I only get about five seconds with someone. In those moments, I have to think on my feet and work with whatever the environment gives me. That’s actually a big reason I’ve been gravitating away from event photography and more toward editorial work these days. There can be a certain lack of intentionality when you’re constantly rushing to capture someone in such a short window of time, and I’ve found myself craving more space to be deliberate with my images. But that’s a rant for another time…What's one of your favorite celebrity portraits you've taken, and what's the story behind it?Ooh. I have favorites for different reasons. I have some favorites because of the photos themselves, like Charlotte Lawrence, Nina Dobrev, and Dennis Rodman. I followed Charlotte out for a cigarette break during a very chaotic, glam fashion week dinner a couple years back, and a paparazzo on the street lit her cigarette with a match, which I thought was fabulous. I shot Dennis Rodman after his debut runway walk for Alexander Wang back in 2023. His look was so sick. I loved the studs on his head. This photo of Nina came to be when we were riding to the CFDAs in 2025. I like how off-the-cuff it was. It was one of like four total images I shot super quickly, but I love the crispness and contrast of the colors. And then in the realm of photos that are favorites because of who the celebrities are and how much I admire them as artists, I have to shoutout the following: my street editorial with Mary Beth Barone, Doechii’s get-ready-with-me style photos, Keke Palmer at the celebration of her Paper Magazine cover, and a night out with Slayyyter."In the words of one of my favorite photographers, Tyrell Hampton, it’s all about energy."Has anyone you've photographed ever surprised you?I don’t know if I’d necessarily categorize it as a surprise, but something I’m always kind of in awe of is how quickly some subjects can “turn it on” in front of a camera and then immediately switch back to just being themselves. It’s fascinating to watch, even if it’s not exactly surprising considering it’s their job. I guess I’m more easily fascinated than surprised at this point in my career.What's the wildest situation you've found yourself in while trying to get a shot?There are a lot… but the time I was riding around Manhattan on a summer night in a gorgeous 1960s convertible from 9 p.m. to 1 a.m., hopping out at different locations around the city to shoot BTS for an editorial, probably takes the cake. It was very “last night was a movie.”Is there a photograph in your archive that holds special meaning to you?So many. My mind immediately goes to the shoots where I had the most creative freedom, specifically ones where I could employ my multimedia editing processes, like Ellie’s Halloween Shoot, Brianna Chickenfry’s Podcast Cover, and the Phe Phe “Sweet on Ya” Campaign.And then there’s, of course, the various botanic series I've been shooting since 2018. I’m obsessed with flowers and anything colorful, so these shots feel like a perfect encapsulation of everything I find beautiful. How has social media changed the way we photograph and look at celebrities?I think social media has really changed what people want to see from celebrities. Celebrity imagery used to feel a lot more polished and out of reach, but now I think people are much more interested in seeing the raw, less curated moments. We’re so used to seeing celebrities through their own Instagram posts that there’s something really fun about getting a glimpse of them through someone else’s lens.Who's someone you've always wanted to photograph but haven't had the chance to?Miley Cyrus. I mean, that’s literally Hannah Montana. And I can’t not mention Drake. If you know me, you know what Drake means to me, so that’s always been a dream.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Artificial Intelligence.title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
Artificial Intelligence.text: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.The benefits of microcredentialsSkills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.Translating standards into microcredentialsBridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Art & Culture.title: Alessio Ascari on What Lasts Once the Hype Dies Down
Art & Culture.text: As the founder of KALEIDOSCOPE and Capsule, Alessio Ascari is one of the few figures in design publishing who translates ideas into physical spaces—from Spazio Maiocchi in Milan and Manifesto in Paris to the annual roaming event Capsule Plaza. This month, Capsule Plaza touches down in Shanghai for the first time, taking over IYOUTH STUDIO from November 10 to 15. Taking advantage of the occasion, Hypebeast sat down with Alessio for an exclusive conversation, spanning his recent observations of Shanghai's design scene, the changing relationship between younger generations and design, and his take on the true motives behind the industry's "crossover" frenzy—ultimately asking: when the hype fades, what is worth holding onto?The Shanghai Design LandscapeYou’ve visited Shanghai frequently recently to prepare for this Capsule Plaza. What excites you most about the current design ecosystem here? Specifically, what shifts are happening that the outside world might not fully realize yet?I really love the energy of Shanghai. What excites me most is the collision between tradition and innovation: cultural heritage and craftsmanship on one side, technological advancement and forward-thinking on the other. There’s also a subcultural and experimental side to Shanghai’s creative scene that outsiders might not be familiar with, but it’s incredibly cool and dynamic. Youth culture is strong here, and people have an international, open mindset, which fills the city with possibilities.Beyond fairs, auctions, and gallery openings, where do you think the most interesting design discussions in Shanghai are happening right now? Could you talk about specific studios, neighborhoods, or individuals?I’m paying close attention to what young creators in Shanghai are doing, especially in design and architecture, where many practice outside the mainstream through independent studios. Mario Tsai is a great example. Seeing an industrial designer like him open his own space to build a platform for his work and ideas is thrilling. I’m also very interested in Atelier Guo and their architectural approach.On the institutional side, I love the cultural programming Prada Rong Zhai is doing; the building itself is stunning. I’ve also been following the work of curator X Zhu-Nowell at the Rockbund Art Museum (RAM), and David Chipperfield’s renovation of the architecture is spot-on.From Milan to Tokyo and Now ShanghaiCapsule Plaza has been held in Milan four times, is heading to Tokyo in 2025, and has now landed in Shanghai. How has your understanding of "design" shifted across these different cities? Placed side-by-side, where does Shanghai sit?The design histories of Milan and Tokyo have many intersections. Especially in the 1980s, as the postmodernist movement evolved, there was a brilliant dialogue between the two cities, which the Memphis Group embodied most vividly.The exchange between Chinese and Italian design and fashion has a similarly long history—take the influence of Chinese aesthetics on Giorgio Armani's collections in the 1980s and 1990s, for example. Today, we are witnessing a new chapter in this cultural exchange, and I hope Capsule Plaza can be part of it.You’ve mentioned that the Capsule model can travel anywhere, but the content is tailored to the location. Bringing it to Shanghai, what are you trying to do differently than in Milan? Facing the need to localize, what elements do you insist on keeping intact?If you think of the Milan edition as the "motherboard," the Shanghai edition is a more compact version—smaller in scale and more agile in its lineup. But our ambition is the same: to connect different fields through interiors, architecture, music, cultural talks, and publishing.Stone Island’s "NO SEASONS" is one of the core threads of this exhibition, featuring an installation by Milanese design studio NM3. Music runs through the entire space, including live DJ sets curated by independent Shanghai radio station BYYB.RADIO. We’ve also invited two contemporary artists to present sculptures exploring the tension between the natural and the artificial, and set up an art gift shop showcasing several design brands and publications from China, Italy, and beyond.But for me, the most important thing is always that "collision and intersection"—bringing people, ideas, and objects that would never normally share a room into the same physical space. The format can adapt to the city, but that core remains unchanged.Milan Design Week is backed by deep historical roots and a mature institutional system, whereas Shanghai is still writing its own design narrative. Does this give you more creative freedom, or does it mean more pressure?Shanghai’s creative forces are booming across multiple dimensions, from projects driven by large cultural institutions to fiercely independent cultural initiatives led by the younger generation. It’s exhilarating to be here at this moment because everything is still full of undefined potential.This openness gives us room to experiment, but it also means we need to connect more deeply with the existing local cultural ecosystem. I want Capsule Plaza to be more than just a showcase; I want it to build bridges, sparking collaborations between local and international creators, brands, and cultural institutions. We brought a format that developed elsewhere, but we want it to engage in Shanghai's local conversations and grow through that exchange.You chose IYOUTH STUDIO in Changning, deliberately avoiding the West Bund art hub. What is the logic behind this location choice, and how does it reflect the way you want audiences to encounter Capsule Plaza? What does the surrounding environment add to the experience you’re trying to create?What drew us to IYOUTH STUDIO was its ability to bring furniture, art, fashion, and contemporary culture together without being confined to any single field. Their aesthetic and way of perceiving things are very close to ours.I love staging Capsule Plaza in a place like this: it inherently flows between different creative fields. Art installations, a professional sound system, DJ performances, cultural talks, a café, and a magazine shop come together to form a complete ecosystem where people can stumble upon unexpected delights.Being away from the core circuit of traditional art fairs gives the venue a completely different rhythm. Visitors can enter through any thread—an installation, music, or a talk—and find their own path of exploration. I love when a project unfolds naturally like that.Cross-Disciplinary IntersectionsWhen we spoke in Milan in 2024, you mentioned that the younger generation was rediscovering design. Two years later, has this trend matured, splintered, or evolved into a new form? What is it becoming?I think people’s connection to design is becoming more personal, even intimate. The pandemic was a major catalyst: it changed our relationship with domestic life and forced us to reexamine the objects and spaces we live with every day.At the same time, vintage culture continues to rise. The younger generation is looking back at the past, discovering its objects and aesthetics, and reinterpreting them in their own way.Design is becoming a way for people to express themselves, build a personal aesthetic, and connect with the things around them. I think this shift goes beyond simply following a trend or collecting a specific piece.The intersection of design, art, architecture, and fashion is practically the norm today. In your view, where is the next truly worthwhile intersection to explore? Are there any directions that haven’t yet been named or widely recognized?I think the hospitality and resort sector is undergoing a transformation. A hotel, a resort, or even an entire travel destination can become a natural meeting point for design, art, architecture, fashion, and food. More and more cultural institutions and brands are doubling down on these spaces, which reflects what people want right now: human connection, a sense of belonging, and the memories formed between people and places.I don’t really like the word "experience" because it’s a bit overused. But one thing is clearer than ever: more than material things, time is the ultimate luxury.You once curated a major exhibition about Virgil Abloh and Gucci. From your perspective, how much of the constantly referenced "crossover" stems from an organic flow between cultures, and how much is just brand marketing disguised as creativity?I can’t imagine being confined to a single framework or field. The people who inspire me most creatively are usually true polymaths. They navigate different dimensions with ease, bringing ideas from one world into another.For me, true cross-disciplinary thinking starts with curiosity and a genuine urge to explore, rather than setting out with a predetermined goal to connect different industries.Of course, brands are getting better at leveraging these intersections strategically. But when the connection itself is authentic, it can still spark a chemistry that transcends the sum of its parts.The Role of the CuratorYou helm Capsule, Kaleidoscope, Spazio Maiocchi, Manifesto in Paris, and Capsule Plaza—what is the core thread tying all these projects together? And what is the biggest tension you have to navigate between them?I’m interested in building cultural platforms rather than staying confined to a single field. Every project has its own unique identity and audience, but they all stem from the same curiosity, pointing toward art, design, fashion, music, and contemporary culture in the broadest sense.Kaleidoscope started in publishing, Spazio Maiocchi is a physical space, and Capsule spans both print and offline events. They each have their own way of operating, but I see them as complementary parts of the same ecosystem, not isolated projects. The biggest challenge is letting each project grow naturally along its own trajectory while maintaining the perspective that connects them. I’ve never had any interest in creating cookie-cutter, interchangeable templates; every project must have an irreplaceable reason to exist.Over the past five years, the design industry has expanded rapidly: fairs are denser, collectible design auctions are breaking records, cross-brand collaborations are endless, and budgets and expectations are skyrocketing. From an operational or cultural logic standpoint, what cognitive biases or misconceptions do you think still exist in the industry today?I think this industry sometimes confuses visibility with cultural value. True, there are more platforms, collaborations, and opportunities now than ever before, but that doesn’t mean we’re creating work with deeper value. We should give things the time they need to develop fully, rather than rushing toward the next launch or the next fleeting trend. Not every collaboration needs to exist, and not every object has to be a collectible.What interests me is getting the right people together for the right reasons, and giving them enough space to make something neither side could achieve alone. I care more about the quality of the ideas themselves than the scale, and what stays with people long after the hype fades.Personal Interests and the FutureLately, what has excited you that lies outside design and its adjacent fields, beyond the usual talking points, yet is quietly influencing your thinking?Sound is vital to me. It’s the energy and inspiration that runs through my day, helping me shift between different moods and atmospheres. I listen to music constantly, and lately, I’ve been digging back into the catalog of the German label ECM; it builds an incredibly nuanced world of jazz and ambient music. I’ve also been revisiting reggae and dub classics from Wackies, as well as quintessential street rap from Griselda.I’m also almost obsessively collecting out-of-print vintage books and independent magazines. Wherever I go, I seek out indie bookstores, publishers, and rare editions. I’m building my own private library, and I go back there every day to find references, organize my thoughts, or, more often than not, just immerse myself completely.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Globe-Trotter and YOSHIROTTEN Split a “SUPERNOVA” Across Three Suitcases
Art & Culture.text: SummaryGlobe-Trotter and YOSHIROTTEN have built a three-piece suitcase set that forms one continuous artwork when the cases stand side by sideThe graphics draw from YOSHIROTTEN’s “SUPERNOVA” work, layering nebula blues, oranges, pinks and greens over the brand’s signature black fiberboardThe release commemorates the artist’s 'BEYOND EARTH' exhibition, currently on view at TOKYO NODE in Tokyo’s Toranomon HillsGlobe-Trotter has teamed up with Tokyo-based artist YOSHIROTTEN on the “SUPERNOVA” suitcase set, a limited trio of hard-shell cases that only reveals its full image when all three pieces are lined up together. Created to mark YOSHIROTTEN’s BEYOND EARTH exhibition, the project translates his large-scale cosmic imagery onto a functional travel object, turning a matching luggage set into a single, modular canvas.Each case starts from Globe-Trotter’s defining material, a black vulcanized fiberboard shell that serves as the dark backdrop for YOSHIROTTEN’s palette. Over that base, the artist stacks bands of blue, orange, pink and green meant to evoke drifting nebulae and distant horizon lines, pulling directly from “SUPERNOVA,” his piece exploring the dramatic life cycles of stars. Because the composition runs continuously across all three shells, no single suitcase tells the whole story, which is why the cases are sold strictly as a set rather than individually.The hardware details lean into longevity. Handles are cut from natural leather that gradually darkens into a rich amber tone with use, so every set will develop its own patina depending on how often it travels. Opening any of the cases reveals YOSHIROTTEN’s handwritten signature on the interior, marking each piece as an authenticated part of the edition.In terms of sizing, every suitcase measures 58cm wide, 42cm tall and 21cm deep, offering 34L of capacity, putting all three cases on identical footprints so the artwork aligns cleanly when displayed. Production is capped at six sets in total, making this one of the more tightly limited art-luggage projects of the year.The collaboration is tied to BEYOND EARTH, which runs from October 30 through January 11, 2027, across TOKYO NODE GALLERY A, B and C inside Toranomon Hills Station Tower.The Globe-Trotter x YOSHIROTTEN “SUPERNOVA” suitcase set releases November 16 via Globe-Trotter’s official online store.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Wicker, Coachwork and Sapphires Take Center Stage at Sotheby’s ‘The Human Touch’
Art & Culture.text: SummarySotheby’s hosts The Human Touch from November 23 – 28, a special exhibition celebrating luxury handcraftsmanship.Highlights include a wicker Hermès Mini Kelly Picnic and Morgan’s Midsummer Coupé.Creations by Charles Frodsham and Moussaieff Jewellers spotlight human artistry.This month, Sotheby’s is presenting The Human Touch, a special exhibition spotlighting the enduring value of handcraftsmanship across the global luxury ecosystem. Bringing together a curated mix of rare automobiles, watches, jewelry and collectibles, the showcase celebrates the human ingenuity and technical mastery behind some of the most sought-after creations on the market in an era increasingly shaped by automation.Leading the presentation is the coveted Hermès Mini Kelly Picnic, a standout example of artisanal savoir-faire that pairs a hand-woven natural wicker body with smooth pale blue-gray leather across its top flap, handle, and signature sangles, finished with silver-tone turn-lock hardware.Anchoring the exhibition’s automotive narrative is British marque Morgan Motor Company, celebrated for over a century of bespoke coachbuilding that blends traditional hand-built techniques with contemporary engineering. Headlining its presence is the one-of-a-kind Morgan Midsummer Coupé “The Artists’ Proof,” showcasing sweeping sculpted fenders, a classic vertical-slat grille, and a sleek enclosed cabin finished in a deep, dark metallic hue.Horological and high-jewelry craftsmanship are equally represented through the Charles Frodsham Double Impulse Chronometer “Hidden Seconds” - distinguished by its crisp white dial, dark blue Arabic numerals, blued-steel hands, and contrast-stitched black leather strap - and an intricate Y-drop necklace from Moussaieff Jewellers that weaves royal blue, purple and pink sapphires into diamond-set ribbons.As James Marks, Sotheby’s SVP and Global Head of Private Sales & Retail, Watches, noted, while the featured objects span vastly different disciplines, “they are united by a common thread: the skill, dedication and artistry of the people who create them.” Serving as a timely reminder that true luxury remains defined by human creativity and meticulous craft even in a tech-driven age, the exhibition will be on view from November 23 - 28, 2026 at Sotheby's Zürich location.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Barry McGee Is Back for ‘Another Round’ with Jeffrey Deitch
Art & Culture.text: SummaryArtist Barry McGee has unveiled a new "solo" exhibition at Jeffrey Deitch's Los Angeles outpost, titled 'Another Round'The exhibition, running through January 30, 2027, features over 200 paintings, sculptures, and photographs by McGee alongside hundreds of works from friends and collaborators, including a mini fabrication of '99CENTS,' his knockout anti-art fair presentation earlier this yearAfter he opened a knockout 99CENT in February, artist Barry McGee is back in Los Angeles for Another Round, his new exhibition at Jeffrey Deitch's Santa Monica Boulevard space. The graffiti writer-turned contemporary art star gathers over 200 paintings, sculptures, and photographs to envelope the space. It's his first show with Deitch in 20 years, and in the spirit of the Frieze anti-fair, was made possible with a little help from his friends.While billed as such, the show is less of a “solo” than a snapshot of McGee's place in the art world: his curatorial style and unique place in high-low culture. “In this day and age, a solo anything seems ridiculous,” he recently told The Los Angeles Times. “The ego of the artist is a tricky thing.”Highlights include a bulbous hang of prints and photographs oozing from the walls of the main gallery and kaleidoscopic tiled works peppered throughout. Crowded between them are works by the likes of CHITO, Chris Lux, Todd James, Tom Franco, C. R. Stecky III, and more, like a painted bench by Alfonzo Gonzalez Jr. and KATSU's incognito tagger, a robotic arm spraying from the inside of a bush.Another Round also includes two mock storefronts — galleries within the gallery — created with fellow artist Alexis Ross. One sees a condensed refabrication of the original 99-cent store, linoleum floor, pegboard shelving, and all, spilling with pieces from the show. The other is a bookshop run by Heavy Manners Library's Matthew James-Wilson, which carries zines, books, T-shirts, and McGee's favorite granola.For the exhibition text, Deitch, the gallerist, reflects on his three-decades-long relationship with McGee, seeing the artist's impact on New York's art and skating scene, and later inviting him to take part in the 2011 street art show at MOCA during his tenure. Alongside the works, the show places a spotlight on the two's creative trust, best summed by McGee when he asked Deitch: “Jeffrey, could you give me the keys?”Another Round by Barry McGee is on view until January 30, 2027.Jeffrey Deitch Los Angeles7000 Santa Monica Blvd.,Los Angeles, CA 90038Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
